UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    Southern Natural Gas Company, LLC                       )                            Docket Nos. CP25-517
    Elba Express Company, LLC                               )
                                                            )
    Tennessee Gas Pipeline Company, LLC                     )                                           CP25-514


                   COMMENTS ON PROJECT NEED AND
                 MOTION FOR EVIDENTIARY HEARING OF
         ALABAMA RIVERS ALLIANCE, BLACKBELT WOMEN RISING,
    ENERGY ALABAMA, GEORGIA INTERFAITH POWER & LIGHT, MARY AVERY,
                  MISSISSIPPI RISING COALITION, AND
                SOUTHERN ALLIANCE FOR CLEAN ENERGY

         Alabama Rivers Alliance, Blackbelt Women Rising, Energy Alabama, Georgia Interfaith

Power & Light, Mary Avery, Mississippi Rising Coalition, and Southern Alliance for Clean

Energy (collectively, “Intervenors”) respectfully submit these comments regarding the alleged

need for the South System Expansion 4 (“SSE4”) and Mississippi Crossing Project (“MSX”)

(collectively, the “Projects”) at issue in the above referenced dockets. It is the statutory

obligation of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”) to

consider whether proposed natural gas projects are supported by market need and the impacts

projects may have on ratepayers. 1

         This filing provides additional, concrete evidence explaining why the utility-supported

precedent agreements cannot be treated as conclusive proof of genuine, project-specific need.

First, Georgia Power's fuel-cost materials show that substantial fixed firm transportation cost

obligations may begin years before associated generating units enter service, that the utility's



1
 See New Jersey Conservation Found. v. FERC, 111 F.4th 42, 58–59 (D.C. Cir. 2024); Env’t Def. Fund v. FERC, 2
F.4th 953, 959–60 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (“Spire”) cert. denied sub nom. Spire Missouri Inc. v. Env’t Def. Fund, 142 S. Ct.

 budget depends on uncertain capacity-sale proceeds to offset a portion of those costs, and that the

current public methodology does not directly assign the fixed firm transportation (“FT”) charges

to the large load customers whose projected demand is invoked to justify the infrastructure—it’s

on residential and smaller customers. Second, South Carolina materials confirm that fuel-

transportation and capacity-related costs may be recovered across broad classes of captive

customers, with residential customers presently bearing a substantial share of specified fuel-

factor components. Third, these state records demonstrate why affiliate contracting, uncertain

large load forecasts, overlapping transportation portfolios, and the ability to seek recovery from

captive customers materially weaken the alleged market need that FERC might otherwise infer

from precedent agreements. Thus, these comments also further demonstrate, in addition to the

substantial evidence already on the record, 2 why the Commission cannot rely on the mere

existence of precedent agreements to determine actual market need for these Projects.

        Intervenors also respectfully move the Commission to hold an evidentiary hearing to

consider whether, in light of this and other substantial record evidence, Project Applicants have

 sufficiently demonstrated market need such that the Commission can support certifying these

Projects to be required by the present or future public convenience and necessity. 3

         The Applicants, Southern Natural Gas Company, L.L.C. (“SNG”), Elba Express

Company, L.L.C. (“EEC”), and Tennessee Gas Pipeline Company, L.L.C. (“TGP”), extensively

rely on executed precedent agreements to demonstrate Project need. 4 Under the Commission's

Certificate Policy Statement and controlling law, while precedent agreements are important

evidence of need, they are not dispositive evidence of need. 5 And where, as here, a substantial

portion of the precedent agreements are with corporate affiliates, the Commission will more

closely scrutinize these agreements and consider them less meaningful indicators of need. 6

         The Commission's scrutiny of affiliate precedent agreements should be informed by the

risk that utility or local distribution company (“LDC”) shippers, or their affiliates, may be able

(and for at least the vast majority of FT contracted in this case, are able) to pass through the costs

of excess FT to captive customers through state-approved fuel-cost, gas-cost, or capacity-

recovery mechanisms. 7 Several of the vertically integrated, investor-owned utility shippers and

affiliates on the Projects are subject to traditional cost-of-service regulations that allow them to

the generation assets enabled by the new pipeline capacity. 8 Because of the scale of proposed

generation build-out enabled by the Projects, these generation assets will not merely be a

marginal increase to ratebase for the anchor shippers bankrolling these Projects—for the leading

utilities in the Southeast fed by this pipeline, the billions worth of proposed generation assets will

        The same uncertain data center and other large load forecasts are being invoked to justify

both multibillion-dollar generation investments and the long-term FT commitments associated

with MSX and SSE4. If those forecasts prove overstated, state cost-recovery mechanisms will

expose residential, small-business, and other captive customers to substantial costs associated

The fact that a large share of fuel cost is allocated to the residential class means that any misstep

by FERC in vetting the need for MSX and SSE4 could shift billions of dollars of cost recovery

for speculative infrastructure onto ratepayers, including potentially onto the smallest.

         As the D.C. Circuit recognized in New Jersey Conservation Foundation, even when the

public record raises serious questions about whether capacity is actually needed, entities serving

captive customers may nevertheless contract for additional capacity. 11 FERC must therefore

meaningfully examine the substantial evidence on the lack of true market need for this proposed

FT capacity and consider that “captive ratepayers might pay for added pipeline capacity

[shippers do] not use to serve those customers. If ratepayers assume the cost even when they do

not need the capacity, [shippers] can afford to contract for additional unneeded capacity, which

they can then resell at a profit, even in a soft capacity market.” 12 Indeed, the Commission's own

Certificate Policy Statement recognizes both the need to protect consumers and the importance

of preventing overbuilding, as it must do so here. 13


I.       Factual Background

     A. The Projects’ Affiliate Shippers & Pathway to FT Cost Recovery from Captive
        Ratepayers for Unneeded Capacity.

         Southern Company, which is a joint owner of SNG, has several corporate affiliates who

are major shippers on SSE4 and MSX. Southern Company Services (“SCS”) is one such affiliate

that handles natural gas commodity and transportation to serve other Southern Company

operating affiliates, including Georgia Power and its corresponding gas-fired generation. 14 SCS

on SSE4 and 600,000 Dth/d on MSX, as well as 400,000 Dth/d on the Southeast Supply

Enhancement Project (“SSEP”), and 800,000 Dth/d on Kosciusko Junction Project (“Kosci”), for

a total of over 2.185 Bcf/d FT capacity. 15 The LEI Evaluation of Demand Report considered the

public load forecasts and resource plans of corporate affiliates that that could be serviced by

Southern Company Services’ (“SCS”) contracted capacity across SSE4, MSX, SSEP, and the

Kosciusko Junction Project (“Kosci”). LEI found that the public record does not support project-

specific need for the FT SCS contracted for on SSE4 and MSX. 16

        In its Motion to Intervene, SCS explained that through its affiliated public utility

subsidiaries, the various Southern Company corporate affiliates “function as a single, vertically

integrated public utility system,” and “own and operate more than 44,000 [megawatts] of electric

generation capacity at various locations throughout the Southeast, a substantial portion of which

is gas-fired.” 17

        One striking example of how fuel cost recovery would work for SCS FT capacity on

SSE4 and MSX is through SCS’s affiliate Georgia Power. Georgia Power’s public record reveals

a substantial disconnect between the large load customers—e.g. data centers—invoked to justify

new gas-fired generation and FT pipeline capacity and the customers currently assigned the fixed

costs of that capacity. Currently, large load customers are effectively insulated from the cost

increases and risks associated with FT, while other customers, including residential and small

businesses, are left on the hook.

         Georgia Power recovers its FT and other gas-pipeline-related costs from retail ratepayers

through its Fuel Cost Recovery (“FCR”) tariff. These costs include those arising from FT

commitments undertaken by Southern Company Services, Inc. on Georgia Power’s behalf. 18

Georgia Power’s FCR schedule is incorporated into the retail rate schedules that reference it, for

example, residential and small business tariffs, and those customer bills are increased by the

Public Service Commission-approved FCR amount. 19

        Georgia’s fuel-cost-recovery rules likewise require electric utilities to file, in both

historical and projected periods, information on fuel and fuel-related contracts, natural gas

contracts, and natural gas transportation contracts, including transportation providers, contract

terms, daily volumes, transport rates, delivery points, and “variable cost components of the total

net recoverable fuel cost for the test year.” 20 Critically, those same rules provide that

“[r]eferences to Utility actions include those which are taken by any affiliates acting on the

Utility’s behalf,” meaning that Georgia Power must also account for—and can recover from—the

actions SCS takes on its behalf. 21

behalf in connection with natural gas contracting. 22 Therefore, if Georgia Power incurs approved

costs from captive ratepayers.

     B. Georgia Power’s Current Recovery Methodology Does Not Allocate Fixed FT to
        Qualifying New Large Loads.

        It was recently established through a public hearing that Georgia Power’s large load

customers are subject to a different tariff that does not include cost recovery from FT on new or

existing gas pipelines. Thus, despite being the stated impetus for Georgia Power’s new natural gas

infrastructure boom, large load customers are not carrying a substantial cost directly related to the

development of interstate gas pipelines regulated by FERC—the cost of FT. Those costs are

currently shifted onto the rest of the ratepayers despite the fact that they are not the “cost causers.”

        In April 2025, the Georgia Public Service Commission (“GA PSC”) approved an order

revising tariffs and service requirements for new large load customers of Georgia Power with an

expected total peak demand of at least 100 megawatts. 23 Among other requirements, these

customers, which include newly connecting large load customers such as data centers, must

purchase all of their energy priced under Georgia Power’s Real Time Pricing (“RTP”) structure. 24

        The record recently developed in the Georgia Power’s 2026 fuel cost recovery proceeding

demonstrates that RTP revenues are not allocated to any FT reservation costs for natural gas

capacity. Simply put, this means that new large load customers including data centers are not

(i.e. non-large-load) customers. 28 This means the FT ratesetting methodology contains no direct

allocation of the fixed gas pipeline reservation charge to the RTP customers whose project demand

is driving the alleged need for additional gas infrastructure.

     C. Georgia Power’s FCR-27 Budget Provides Additional, Substantial Evidence on
        Ratepayer Risks from Pipeline Development, FT Recovery Mechanisms, and
        Associated Large Load Growth.

         Georgia Power's FCR-27 budget provides a concrete example of why the allocation issue

bears on the evidentiary weight of SCS's precedent agreements. The budget identifies a large FT

obligation that begins before several associated generating units enter service, assumes substantial

offsetting capacity-sale proceeds, and contains no direct allocation of FT to large load customers.

Georgia Power’s new FT costs include transportation costs associated with new combustion

        And while the budget shows that Georgia Power assumes that much of these charges will

be recovered through capacity sales, Georgia Power leaves captive customers bearing all the risk

if those sales fail to recover the full $73 million of gas capacity. This is because Georgia Power

remains contractually responsible for the fixed charges regardless of whether or not it successfully

remarkets the capacity at the assumed price. And because the FCR tariff does not apply to large

load customers, the budget thus exposes residents, small businesses, and other non-data center

customers to potentially substantial under-recovery costs for any number of reasons, including if

less capacity is sold than projected, the capacity is sold for less than its underlying fixed cost, sales

begin later than assumed, counterparties default, operational or tariff constraints limit capacity

release revenues, or market demand for released capacity is weak. Additionally, nothing in the

budget itself demonstrates that Georgia Power has executed binding capacity-release transactions

        5. What receipt-point, delivery-point, pressure, timing, nomination, or tariff
          constraints allegedly prevent those resources from satisfying the asserted need?
          Applicants should quantify each limitation rather than rely on generalized
          assertions concerning geographic diversity or reliability.
       6. Has the same forecasted load growth, generation addition, or reliability need been
          used to support more than one pipeline commitment? If so, how have shippers on
          the Projects avoided double-counting that need?
c. Large load forecasts and realization risk
       1. What specific data center and other large load projects support the demand
          attributed to each shipper and/or their operating affiliate?
       2. What attrition, duplication, delay, downsizing, efficiency, and cancellation
          assumptions are incorporated into the load forecast used to justify the
          transportation commitments?
       3. What is the required SSE4/MSX capacity under alternative scenarios in which
          25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of forecasted large load materializes, and under
          scenarios in which energization is delayed by two, five, or ten years?
d. Fixed costs, cost recovery, and capacity-sale assumptions
       1. What fixed reservation charges, commodity charges, fuel-retention obligations,
          and surcharges would each operating company incur through SCS for SSE4 and
          MSX?
       2. Through what state-approved mechanism does each operating company expect to
          seek recovery of those costs?
       3. For Georgia Power, are fixed FT reservation charges directly allocated to RTP or
          other large load customers? If not, what portion of those charges is expected to be
          recovered from FCR customers?
       4. Has any RTP or other large load customer agreed to reimburse Georgia Power for
          fixed FT charges or stranded costs if its anticipated load is delayed, reduced, or
          cancelled?
       5. For capacity that SCS or an operating affiliate expects to release, remarket, or use
          for off-system sales:
               i. what quantity is expected to be available;
              ii. for what months and years;
             iii. are binding release or sales agreements already executed;
             iv. what revenues are projected;
              v. are the projected revenues gross or net of fixed reservation costs;
             vi. how are revenues or margins credited to ratepayers;



                                           25
             vii. who receives any upside above the fixed cost; and
           viii. who bears any shortfall below the projected amount?
      6. Does the expectation that substantial quantities will be released or remarketed
         indicate that the capacity will not be required to serve native or committed load
         during those periods? If Applicants contend it does not, what reliability or
         operational need justifies paying year-round fixed charges for capacity expected
         to be sold?
e. Affiliate contracting and commercial discipline
      1. What alternatives did shippers evaluate before entering the SSE4 and MSX
         commitments, including existing FT, SSEP, Kosciusko, delivered supply, storage,
         capacity release, and shorter-term service?
      2. What quantitative analysis demonstrated that SSE4 and MSX were the least-cost
         or otherwise preferable portfolio options?
      3. What bids were submitted in the relevant open seasons, how were bids evaluated,
         and did unaffiliated bidders seek comparable service?
      4. What internal Southern Company approvals, utility-prudence analyses, board
         approvals, or state regulatory approvals supported the commitments?
      5. What financial consequences would SCS and other shippers or their shareholders
         bear if the forecasted end-use demand does not materialize, as distinguished from
         amounts that can be recovered from operating affiliates or their captive
         customers?
f. Project economics and FERC’s no-subsidy inquiry
      1. What portion of each Project’s cost is supported by enforceable shipper revenues,
         and what portion would remain unsupported if quantities are reduced, assigned,
         released, or not renewed?
      2. Could any project cost, revenue deficiency, or underutilized capacity be shifted to
         SNG’s, EEC’s, or TGP’s existing jurisdictional customers through rolled-in rates,
         future NGA section 4 filings, fuel charges, surcharges, or other mechanisms?
      3. What certificate and rate conditions are necessary to ensure that:
              i. existing jurisdictional customers do not subsidize the Projects;
             ii. applicants remain at risk for unsubscribed or underutilized capacity;
             iii. affiliate transactions do not transfer project risks to existing customers;
                  and
             iv. future rolled-in treatment is unavailable absent a separate evidentiary
                 showing?
      4. Is each Project independently needed and financially viable if the other Project is
         delayed, reduced, or not constructed?


                                            26
       g. Market economics

            1. How do the fuel-related cost recovery mechanisms in the affected states affect the
               utility incentive structure with respect to pipeline firm transportation price
               negotiation?

            2. To what extent does the combination of fuel-related cost recovery mechanisms,
               affiliate contract agreements, and lack of negotiated rate contract transparency
               reduce the probative weight that could be assigned to the precedent agreements as
               evidence of need?

IV.      Specific Relief Requested
      As demonstrated herein, FERC should initiate an evidentiary hearing in order to test the

credibility of the Applicants’ assertions, garner substantial evidence to make its requisite

evaluation of significant public benefit, and balance those findings against evidence of adverse

economic impacts that it will discover. An ALJ, by providing an opportunity for discovery and

cross-examination, can test credibility and marshal the evidence ultimately deemed credible into

a cohesive picture showing why there is no true public need for these Projects. Because the

record does not contain the currently lacking substantial evidence of significant public benefit,

absent such an evidentiary hearing that could produce credible evidence, the Commission must

deny the Applicants’ application. Intervenors respectfully request FERC to initiate an evidentiary

hearing that can develop such a record for its ultimate determination regarding Applicants’

request for a certificate of public convenience and necessity and weigh the value of such

evidence. 90




 In the alternative, the Commission could issue a data request to the Applicants to obtain this information, but that

would not allow stakeholders to test the veracity of those responses in a meaningful fashion.

Fuel Cost Recovery
Georgia Power has established fuel cost recovery rates approved by the Georgia PSC. During 2022, Georgia Power’s under recovered fuel
balance increased significantly due to higher fuel and purchased power costs. In 2023, the Georgia PSC approved a stipulation between
Georgia Power and the staff of the Georgia PSC to increase annual fuel billings by 54%, or approximately $1.1 billion, effective June 1,
2023. The increase includes a three-year recovery period for $2.2 billion of Georgia Power’s under recovered fuel balance at May 31,
2023. Under the approved stipulation, Georgia Power is allowed to adjust its fuel cost recovery rates under an interim fuel rider (IFR)
prior to the next fuel case, subject to a maximum 40% cumulative change, if its under or over recovered fuel balance accumulated
since May 31, 2023 exceeds $200 million (IFR Threshold). On May 14, 2025, Georgia Power submitted an IFR notification and plan
informing the Georgia PSC that Georgia Power’s under recovered fuel balance exceeded the IFR Threshold. Georgia Power proposed
no fuel cost recovery rate change and was required to monitor and report to the Georgia PSC monthly as long as the under recovered
fuel balance was above the IFR Threshold. Georgia Power filed an IFR notification and plan monthly through September 2025, each of
which also proposed no fuel cost recovery rate change. Between September 30, 2025 and November 30, 2025, Georgia Power’s under
recovered fuel balance did not exceed the IFR Threshold. On each of January 15, 2026 and February 13, 2026, Georgia Power filed an
IFR notification and plan informing the Georgia PSC that Georgia Power’s under recovered fuel balance exceeded the IFR Threshold as of
December 31, 2025 and January 31, 2026, respectively, and proposed no fuel cost recovery rate change. On February 17, 2026, Georgia
Power filed a request with the Georgia PSC to decrease fuel rates by 12.6% effective June 1, 2026, which is expected to reduce annual
billings by approximately $388 million. Georgia Power expects the Georgia PSC to make a final decision on this matter on May 28, 2026.
The ultimate outcome of this matter cannot be determined at this time.

3. RATE AND OTHER REGULATORY MATTERS
Regulatory Matters Involving Potential Loss Contingencies
As a result of issues generated in the ordinary course of business, DESC is involved in various regulatory matters. Certain regulatory matters may ultimately
result in a loss; however, as such matters are in an initial procedural phase, involve uncertainty as to the outcome of pending reviews or orders and/or involve
significant factual issues that need to be resolved, it is not possible for DESC to estimate a range of possible loss. For regulatory matters that DESC cannot
estimate, a statement to this effect is made in the description of the matter. Other matters may have progressed sufficiently through the regulatory process such
that DESC is able to estimate a range of possible loss. For regulatory matters that DESC is able to reasonably estimate a range of possible losses, an estimated
range of possible loss is provided, in excess of the accrued liability (if any) for such matters. Any estimated range is based on currently available information,
involves elements of judgment and significant uncertainties and may not represent DESC’s maximum possible loss exposure. The circumstances of such
regulatory matters will change from time to time and actual results may vary significantly from the current estimate. For current matters not specifically
reported below, management does not anticipate that the outcome from such matters would have a material effect on DESC’s financial position, liquidity or
results of operations.
Other Regulatory Matters
Electric – Base Rate Case
In January 2026, DESC filed its retail electric base rate case and schedules with the South Carolina Commission. DESC proposed a non-fuel, base rate increase
of $331 million, partially offset by a net decrease in storm damage and DSM components of $9 million. If approved, the overall proposed rate increase of $322
million, or 12.7%, would be effective on and after the first billing cycle of July 2026. The base rate increase was proposed to recover the continued investment
in assets and operating resources required to serve DESC’s rapidly expanding customer base and evolving customer needs, while maintaining the safety,
reliability, resiliency and efficiency of its system, and to meet increasingly stringent reliability, security and environmental requirements. DESC presented an
ROE of 4.78% based upon a fully-adjusted test period. The proposed rates would provide for an earned ROE of 10.50% compared to the currently authorized
ROE of 9.94%. This matter is pending.
Electric – Cost of Fuel
DESC’s retail electric rates include a cost of fuel component approved by the South Carolina Commission which may be adjusted periodically to reflect
changes in the price of fuel purchased by DESC.
In February 2025, DESC filed with the South Carolina Commission a proposal to increase the total fuel cost component of retail electric rates. DESC’s
proposed adjustment is designed to recover DESC’s current base fuel costs, including its existing under-collected balance, over the 12-month period beginning
with the first billing cycle of May 2025. In addition, DESC proposed an increase to its variable environmental and avoided capacity cost component. The net
effect is a proposed annual increase of $154 million. In March 2025, DESC and the ORS filed a settlement agreement with the South Carolina Commission for
approval to make certain adjustments to the February 2025 filing that would result in an inconsequential change to the proposed annual increase. In April 2025,
the South Carolina Commission approved the settlement agreement, with rates effective with the first billing cycle of May 2025.
In February 2026, DESC filed with the South Carolina Commission a proposal to increase the total fuel cost component of retail electric rates. DESC’s
proposed adjustment is designed to recover DESC’s current base fuel costs, including its existing under-collected balance, over the 12-month period beginning
with the first billing cycle of May 2026. In addition, DESC proposed an update to its variable environmental and avoided capacity cost component. The net
effect is a proposed annual increase of $36 million. This matter is pending.
Canadys Station
In December 2025, DESC and Santee Cooper filed an application with the South Carolina Commission for approval of a CPCN to jointly construct and operate
Canadys Station. Upon completion, DESC and Santee Cooper will each own a 50% undivided interest in the generating station and its electrical output. The
application included an expected total cost of approximately $5 billion, excluding financing costs, with costs split equally between the joint owners for the
proposed 2.2 GW facility. In addition, the application seeks approval for the construction of a new 230 kV switchyard and related transmission facilities which
are expected to cost approximately $100 million, to be jointly owned by DESC and Santee Cooper, with costs split between the joint owners based on a formula
reflecting shared use. If approved, Canadys Station and related facilities are expected to be placed into service in 2033. The estimated cost and project timelines
are subject to refinement through the permitting process and the negotiation of contracts for major construction suppliers. This matter is pending.
Electric Transmission Project
In December 2024, DESC filed an application with the South Carolina Commission requesting approval of a CPCN to construct and operate the Ritter-
Yemassee Transmission Line #2, comprised of a 17-mile 230 kV transmission line and associated facilities in

 Colleton and Hampton Counties, South Carolina with an estimated total project cost of $55 million. In April 2025, the South Carolina Commission approved
the application.
Electric – Other
DESC has approval for a DSM rider through which it recovers expenditures related to its DSM programs. In January 2025, DESC filed an application with the
South Carolina Commission seeking approval to recover $46 million of costs and net lost revenues associated with these programs, along with an incentive to
invest in such programs. DESC requested that rates be effective with the first billing cycle of May 2025. In April 2025, the South Carolina Commission
approved the request, effective with the first billing cycle of May 2025. In January 2026, DESC filed an application with the South Carolina Commission
seeking approval to recover $54 million of costs and net lost revenues associated with these programs, along with an incentive to invest in such programs.
DESC requested that rates be effective with the first billing cycle of May 2026. This matter is pending.
DESC utilizes a pension costs rider approved by the South Carolina Commission which is designed to allow recovery of projected pension costs, including
under-collected balances or net of over-collected balances, as applicable. The rider is typically reviewed for adjustment every 12 months with any resulting
increase or decrease going into effect beginning with the first billing cycle in May. In February 2025, DESC requested that the South Carolina Commission
approve an adjustment to this rider to decrease annual revenue by $13 million. In April 2025, the South Carolina Commission approved the request. In February
2026, DESC requested that the South Carolina Commission approve an adjustment to this rider to increase annual revenue by $7 million. This matter is
pending.
Natural Gas Rates
DESC’s natural gas tariffs include a PGA that provides for the recovery of actual gas costs incurred, including transportation costs. DESC’s gas rates are
calculated using a methodology which may adjust the cost of gas monthly based on a 12-month rolling average, and its gas purchasing policies and practices are
reviewed annually by the South Carolina Commission.
In June 2025, DESC filed with the South Carolina Commission its monitoring report for the 12-month period ended March 31, 2025 with a total revenue
requirement of $596 million. This revenue requirement represents a $17 million base rate increase under the terms of the Natural Gas Rate Stabilization Act
effective with the first billing cycle of November 2025. In September 2025, the South Carolina Commission approved a total revenue requirement of $594
million, representing a $15 million base rate increase after certain adjustments, effective with the first billing cycle of November 2025.

                                         Il.        FINDINGS OF FACT

    Under the draft terms and conditions, customers would pay the higher of tariffed rates or a
minimum bill amount each billing period they are a customer. If the customer ended the contract
early, the customer would be liable for the minimum bill amounts (not tariffed rate amounts) for
each period for the remaining term of the contract. The tariffed rates would be subject to future
review and modification by the Commission using normal ratemaking processes. However, the
minimum bill amounts would not.

     The Company has provided Staff with a framework for determining minimum bills, but not a
 definitive calculation that Staff can replicate. Under this framework, the minimum bill amounts
 would be set to recover the transmission and generation costs being incurred to serve the new
 large-load customers. Conceptually, this framework appears to be reasonable; however, Staff has
 not yet seen how the Company intends to apply the framework in practice. Due to the uncertainty
 of how the framework will be applied, Staff cannot determine whether the minimum                                bill
 framework will actually result in amounts that are reasonable and appropriate without reviewing
 the actual amounts negotiated for customers.

     Staff recommended that the Commission issue an order approving the revised tariffs with the
 following provisions:

 should Staff deem such recommendation appropriate.

Commission approve Staffs recommendation as a fair resolution of the issues presented in the
Georgia Power Company’s Revision to Rules and Regulations Tariff Compliance Filing.

    At its April 15, 2025, Administrative        Session, the Commission         voted to approve   Staff's
recommendation.

tariffs and the large load contracting framework for the terms and conditions implementing the
revisions to the Company’s Rules and Regulations as approved in the Revision Approval Order.

recommend that the rates be increased should Staff deem such recommendation appropriate.

rates as allowed under Georgia law.

        ORDERED FURTHER, that the terms and conditions of each large load contract
including the minimum bill, termination, and collateral provisions will apply the framework in the
same manner as provided and demonstrated to Staff. To the extent that the actual language in a
contract differs from the language in the draft terms and conditions provided to Staff, Staff may
object to such language if Staff deems that such modification is substantive and does not
adequately protect existing customers from bearing any of the costs of adding the customer. The
terms and conditions shall include language that if the tariffed rates are increased then the customer
will be responsible for paying the new higher rates.

        ORDERED FURTHER, that Staff reserves the ability to review how the large load
contracting framework and the minimum bill methodology implementing the revisions to the
Company’s Rules and Regulations is applied in practice and Staff may object to a minimum bill
amount if Staff deems that it is insufficient.

documentation demonstrating that the contract complies with the requirements of the Revision

  1                          II.     OVERVIEW OF THE FILING

 2   Q.   PLEASE       EXPLAIN        WHY       THE      COMPANY          IS       SEEKING   AN
 3        ADJUSTMENT TO ITS FUEL COST RECOVERY RATES AT THIS TIME.

 4   A.   The Commission’s May 25, 2023 Order Adopting Stipulation in Docket No. 44902
 5        (“FCR-26 Order”) requires Georgia Power to file new FCR rates on or before
 6        February 28, 2026. In compliance with the Commission’s FCR-26 Order, the
 7        Company is proposing to adjust its current fuel rates with the rates set forth in the
 8        FCR-27 Application and supporting minimum filing requirements (“MFRs”) filed
 9        in this docket on February 17, 2026.

10   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF THE COMPANY’S FILING.

11   A.   Georgia Power utilizes a diverse fleet of generation resources to economically and
12        reliably meet the energy needs of its customers. The Company recovers the cost of
13        the fuel that it uses to generate electricity, as well as the cost to purchase energy
14        from various resources – including natural gas and renewable resources, through
15        the Company’s fuel rates. The fuel costs incurred by the Company, by statute, are
16        directly passed through to customers.

17        With this filing, the Company is proposing to adjust its current fuel rates to set fuel
18        rates at an appropriate level to recover the Company’s future fuel costs and
19        projected under-recovery of FCR-26, as projected in the two-year FCR-27 test
20        period from June 1, 2026 through May 31, 2028. Based on the recovery of
21        previously incurred fuel costs over the three-year period as approved by the
22        Commission in the previous FCR-26 proceeding, virtually all of that substantial
23        balance is projected to be collected by May 31, 2026. Consequently, the Company
24        will lower rates for customers as reflected in this filing.

25        Based on average annual fuel rates, the proposed FCR-27 rate changes are projected
26        to decrease the monthly bill of a typical residential customer using an average of
27        1,000 kWh per month by approximately $5.74. Contemporaneous with this fuel rate

                     Direct Testimony of Adam D. Houston and Matthew S. Berrigan
                                  On behalf of Georgia Power Company
                                           Docket No. 56765
                                               Page 3 of 26
  1        filing, the Company has also filed a Storm Damage Recovery Application. Taken
 2        together, these filings will result in a reduction of customer bills by $1.32 per month
 3        for a typical residential customer.

 4        Additionally, as a part of this filing, the Company recommends modifying the
 5        Interim Fuel Recovery Mechanism (“IFR”) to better align the IFR threshold to the
 6        magnitude of the total fuel expenses incurred by the Company on an annual basis.
 7        This modification will provide greater rate stability for customers by allowing FCR
 8        rates set in this filing to absorb natural fuel price volatility and normal fluctuations
 9        in the fuel over- or under-recovery balances on a monthly basis.

10        Finally, the Company proposes to expand its natural gas hedging program by
11        increasing both the percentage of budgeted burn that may be hedged and the length
12        of the hedging window. This expansion is warranted given the projected growth in
13        natural gas burn in the Company’s budget. By enhancing the scope of the hedging
14        program, the Company will be better positioned to mitigate exposure to price
15        fluctuations and provide greater stability in fuel costs for the benefit of customers.

16   Q.   WHAT IS DRIVING THE NEED TO REDUCE THE COMPANY’S FUEL
17        RATES?

18   A.   The proposed decrease in fuel rates is primarily driven by the continued recovery
19        of $2.2 billion of previously under-recovered fuel balance from FCR-26, as
20        expected, with the remaining balance at $310 million as of December 2025. Based
21        on the 2026 Energy Budget included in this filing, virtually all the remaining
22        balance is expected to be collected by May 2026, prior to the implementation of the
23        new fuel rates on June 1, 2026.

24        This decrease is partially offset by the under-recovery of fuel expenses accumulated
25        since the FCR-26 rate went into effect on June 1, 2023, which is $212 million as of
26        December 2025, and is projected to grow to $300 million by May 31, 2026. The
27        FCR-26 under-recovery is primarily driven by higher levels of coal generation, and


                     Direct Testimony of Adam D. Houston and Matthew S. Berrigan
                                  On behalf of Georgia Power Company
                                           Docket No. 56765
                                               Page 4 of 26
  1        actual natural gas prices that were lower than what was projected in Real-Time
 2        Pricing (“RTP”) revenues in the FCR-26 budget. In addition, there are increasing
 3        fuel expenses in the forecasted periods primarily driven by projected increase in
 4        natural gas prices compared to the natural gas price update incorporated for fuel
 5        rates in FCR-26 and the higher load requirement projected in the test period. We
 6        explain these factors in greater detail later in this testimony.

 7        Even with these factors putting upward pressure on rates, the recovery of prior
 8        under-recovered fuel balance more than offsets these items and the result is a net
 9        decrease to customers of $388 million on an annual basis, as shown in
10        Exhibit___(ADH/MSB-7), Page 1. As a result, the Company seeks to adjust its fuel
11        rates to recover its projected fuel costs for the FCR-27 test period as further
12        described below.

          is defined   as “any retail supplier of electricity subject to the rate-making jurisdiction of the

          Recovery (“FCR”) proposal, which is to be held no less than 10 days after the utility's filing. Not later
          than 90 days after the utility's filing, this Commission must issue an order that states the base fuel
          rates to be used by the utility during the next three consecutive calendar months, or until changed as
          provided in law. If such an order is not issued within this timeframe, the fuel rates proposed by the
          utility become effective by operation of law. O.C.G.A. § 46-2-26(e).

The Georgia Public Service Commission Public Interest Advocacy Staff (“PIA Staff’), Georgia
Power Company (“Georgia Power” or the “Company”), and the undersigned Intervening Parties
(collectively, “Stipulating Parties”) agree to the following Stipulation as a resolution to the
Company’s requests in Docket No. 56765, Georgia Power’s Fuel Cost Recovery Application
(FCR-27), and Docket No. 44280, Georgia Power Company’s Storm Damage Recovery
Application.

                                         Fuel Cost Recovery

 1.    Georgia Power’s       Applications   are       accepted   as filed,   except   as modified   by   this
       Stipulation.

 2.    The test period in FCR-27 shall be set as June 1, 2026 to May 31, 2028.

 3.    The Company agrees to a reduction of the FCR-27 fuel balance by $13.0 million as of
       May 31, 2026.

 4.    The Commission makes no finding of prudence, imprudence, or disallowance regarding
       any of the generating plant outages from the FCR-27 historic period.

 5.    The Interim Fuel Rider (“IFR”) mechanism shall be modified as follows:

           a.     The maximum amount by which fuel rates can be adjusted during an FCR cycle
                  (1.e., the period between fuel cases) is 40% above or below the approved FCR-27
                  rates;

                shall, within five days of its IFR notification filing, submit for Commission
                consideration a proposed IFR rate adjustment to amortize the over- or under-
                recovered balance over a reasonable and financially prudent period of time. Such
                proposed rate adjustment will be approved, modified, or rejected at the

                                                                    APPLICABILITY

   This adjustment is applicable to and is part of the Utility's South Carolina retail electric rate schedules.

   The fuel, variable environmental & avoided capacity, and DER avoided costs, to be recovered in an amount rounded to the nearest one-
   thousandth of a cent per kilowatt-hour, will be determined by the following formulas:

                      FC =       EF     +   GF
                                 S          S1
                     FEC = EEC + GEC
                               S2
                     FAC = EAC + GAC
                               S2

     Total Fuel Rate
            per kWh =            FC     + FEC +           FAC

   Where:

   FC =        Fuel cost per kilowatt-hour included in base rate, rounded to the nearest one-thousandth of a cent.

   EF =        Total projected system fuel costs:

                      (A) Fuel consumed in the Utility's own plants and the Utility's share of fuel consumed in jointly owned or leased plants.
                          The cost of fossil fuel shall include no items other than those listed in Account 151 of the Commission's Uniform
                          System of Accounts for Public Utilities and Licensees. The cost of nuclear fuel shall be that as shown in Account 518
                          excluding rental payments on leased nuclear fuel and except that, if Account 518 also contains any expense for fossil
                          fuel which has already been included in the cost of fossil fuel, it shall be deducted from this account.


                                                                          PLUS
                      (B) Fuel costs related to purchased power such as those incurred in unit power and limited term power purchases where
                          the fossil fuel costs associated with energy purchased are identifiable and are identified in the billing statement, and
                          also including avoided energy costs incurred by the Utility. Also, the cost of "firm generation capacity purchases,"
                          which are defined as purchases made to cure a capacity deficiency or to maintain adequate reserve levels. Costs of
                          "firm generation capacity purchases" includes the total delivered costs of firm generation capacity purchased and
                          excludes generation capacity reservation charges, generation capacity option charges and any other capacity charges.


                                                                          PLUS
                      (C) Fuel costs related to purchased power (including transmission charges), such as short term, economy and other such
                          purchases, where the energy is purchased on an economic dispatch basis, including the total delivered cost of
                          economy purchases of electric power defined as purchases made to displace higher cost generation at a cost which is
                          less than the purchasing Utility's avoided variable costs for the generation of an equivalent quantity of electric power.


                           Energy receipts that do not involve money payments such as diversity energy and payback of storage energy are not
                           defined as purchased or interchange power relative to this fuel calculation.

                                                                          MINUS
                      (D) The cost of fuel recovered through intersystem sales including the fuel costs related to economy energy sales and
                          other energy sold on an economic dispatch basis.

                           Energy deliveries that do not involve billing transactions such as diversity energy and payback of storage energy are
                           not defined as sales relative to this fuel calculation.

   S=          Projected system kilowatt-hour sales excluding any intersystem sales.

   GF =        Cumulative difference between jurisdictional fuel revenues billed and fuel expenses at the end of the month preceding the
               projected period utilized in EF and S.

   S1 =        Projected jurisdictional kilowatt-hour sales, for the period covered by the fuel costs included in E F.

   FEC =       Customer class variable environmental and avoided capacity costs per kilowatt-hour included in base rates, rounded to the
               nearest one-thousandth of a cent.

                                                        AVAILABILITY

This rider is available in conjunction with the Company’s Retail Electric Service Rates, for a Customer-Generator who applies
for NEM service from May 17, 2019, through May 31, 2021. The customer’s generating system must be manufactured, installed
and operated in accordance with governmental and industry standards and must fully conform with the Company’s current
interconnection standards as approved by the Public Service Commission of South Carolina.


                                                  CHARACTER OF SERVICE

The applicable character of service is specific to the rate schedule that the customer receives service under.

                                                      RATE PER MONTH

The applicable rate per month shall be from the appropriate rate schedule as referenced in the availability section above. The
monthly bill shall be determined as follows:

For electric service under a time-of-use rate schedule:

    1.   The basic facilities charge shall be determined and billed as set forth in the applicable rate schedule as described in
         the Availability section above.

    2.   Any demand charges shall be determined and billed as set forth in the applicable rate schedule as described in the
         Availability section above.

    3.   If a customer-generator’s energy consumption exceeds the electricity provided by the customer-generator during a
         monthly billing period, the customer-generator shall be billed in kWh for the net electricity supplied by the Utility.

         If a customer-generator’s energy generation exceeds the electricity provided by the Utility during a monthly billing
         period, the customer-generator shall be credited for the excess kWh generated during that billing period.

         Energy charges (or credits) shall be based on the rates in the applicable rate schedules as described in the availability
         section above. For on-peak energy, the customer’s monthly usage amount in kilowatt-hours shall be reduced by the
         total of (a) any on-peak excess energy delivered to the Company in the current month plus (b) any accumulated on-
         peak excess energy balance remaining from prior months. Total on-peak energy in kilowatt-hours billed to customers
         shall never be less than zero. For off-peak energy, the customer’s monthly usage shall be reduced by the total of (a)
         any off-peak excess energy delivered to the Company in the current month plus (b) any accumulated off-peak excess
         energy balance remaining from prior months plus (c) any accumulated on-peak excess energy balance from the current
         month or prior months that was not used to reduce on-peak usage. Total off-peak energy in kilowatt-hours billed to
         customers shall also never be less than zero. For any billing month during which excess energy exceeds the customer’s
         usage in total, producing a net credit, the respective energy charges for the billing month shall be zero. Any excess
         energy credits shall carry forward on the following month’s bill by first applying excess on-peak kWh against on-peak
         kWh charges and excess off-peak kWh against off-peak kWh charges, then applying any remaining on-peak kWh
         against any remaining off-peak kWh charges. Credits shall not offset the basic facilities charge or the demand charge
         for the applicable rate schedule.

    4.   Excess energy not used in the current billing month to reduce billed kWh usage shall be accumulated and used to
         reduce usage in future months. For all affected billing statements rendered during November billing cycles, any
         accumulated excess energy not used to reduce billed kWh usage shall be paid to the customer-generator at the
         Company’s avoided cost, zeroing out the customer generator’s account of excess energy. The avoided cost is the off-
         peak winter energy credit as approved in the Company’s Rate PR-1, Small Power Production and Cogeneration
         schedule.

                                                      MINIMUM CHARGE

The monthly minimum charge shall be the basic facilities charge plus the demand charge, if any, as stated in the applicable rate.

                                                         DEFINITIONS

    1.   Customer-Generator means the owner, operator, lessee, or customer-generator lessee of an electric energy generation
         unit which:

            (A) generates or discharges electricity from a Renewable Energy Resource, including an energy storage device
            configured to receive electrical charge solely from an onsite Renewable Energy Resource;
            (B) has an electrical generating system with a capacity of:
                   (i) not more than the lesser of one thousand kilowatts (1,000 kW AC) or one hundred percent (100%) of
                   contract demand if a non-residential customer; or
                   (ii) not more than twenty kilowatts (20 kW AC) if a residential customer;
            (C) is located on a single premises owned, operated, leased, or otherwise controlled by the customer;
            (D) is interconnected and operates in parallel phase and synchronization with an electrical utility and complies with
            the applicable interconnection standards;
            (E) is intended primarily to offset part or all of the customer-generator's own electrical energy requirements; and
            (F) meets all applicable safety, performance, interconnection, and reliability standards established by the
            commission, the National Electrical Code, the National Electrical Safety Code, the Institute of Electrical and
            Electronics Engineers, Underwriters Laboratories, the federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and any local
            governing authorities.

    2.   Renewable Energy Resource means solar photovoltaic and solar thermal resources, wind resources, hydroelectric
         resources, geothermal resources, tidal and wave energy resources, recycling resources, hydrogen fuel derived from
         renewable resources, combined heat and power derived from renewable resources, and biomass resources.

For electric service under a standard, non time-of-use rate schedule:

    1.   The basic facilities charge shall be determined and billed as set forth in the applicable rate schedule as described in
         the Availability section above.

    2.   Any demand charges shall be determined and billed as set forth in the applicable rate schedule as described in the
         Availability section above.

    3.   If a customer-generator’s energy consumption exceeds the electricity provided by the customer-generator during a
         monthly billing period, the customer-generator shall be billed in kWh for the net electricity supplied by the Utility.

         If a customer-generator’s energy generation exceeds the electricity provided by the Utility during a monthly billing
         period, the customer-generator shall be credited for the excess kWh generated during that billing period.

         Energy charges (or credits) shall be based on the rates in the applicable rate schedules as described in the availability
         section above. For purposes of calculating monthly energy, the customer’s usage shall be reduced by the total of (a)
         any excess energy delivered to the Company in the current month plus (b) any accumulated excess energy balance
         remaining from prior months. Total energy in kilowatt-hours billed to customers shall never be less than zero. For any
         billing month during which excess energy exceeds the customer’s usage in total, producing a net credit, the respective
         energy charges for the billing month shall be zero. Credits shall not offset the basic facilities charge or the demand
         charge for the applicable rate schedule.

    4.   Excess energy not used in the current billing month to reduce billed kWh usage shall be accumulated and used to
         reduce usage in future months. For all affected billing statements rendered during November billing cycles, any
         accumulated excess energy not used to reduce billed kWh usage shall be paid to the customer-generator at the
         Company’s avoided cost, zeroing out the customer generator’s account of excess energy. The avoided cost is the off-
         peak winter energy credit as approved in the Company’s Rate PR-1, Small Power Production and Cogeneration
         schedule.

                                                      MINIMUM CHARGE

The monthly minimum charge shall be the basic facilities charge plus the demand charge, if any, as stated in the applicable rate.

                                                         DEFINITIONS

    1.   Customer-Generator means the owner, operator, lessee, or customer-generator lessee of an electric energy generation
         unit which:

            (A) generates or discharges electricity from a Renewable Energy Resource, including an energy storage device
            configured to receive electrical charge solely from an onsite Renewable Energy Resource;
            (B) has an electrical generating system with a capacity of:
                   (i) not more than the lesser of one thousand kilowatts (1,000 kW AC) or one hundred percent (100%) of
                   contract demand if a non-residential customer; or
                   (ii) not more than twenty kilowatts (20 kW AC) if a residential customer;
            (C) is located on a single premises owned, operated, leased, or otherwise controlled by the customer;
            (D) is interconnected and operates in parallel phase and synchronization with an electrical utility and complies with
            the applicable interconnection standards;
            (E) is intended primarily to offset part or all of the customer-generator's own electrical energy requirements; and
            (F) meets all applicable safety, performance, interconnection, and reliability standards established by the
            commission, the National Electrical Code, the National Electrical Safety Code, the Institute of Electrical and
            Electronics Engineers, Underwriters Laboratories, the federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and any local
            governing authorities.

    2.   Renewable Energy Resource means solar photovoltaic and solar thermal resources, wind resources, hydroelectric
         resources, geothermal resources, tidal and wave energy resources, recycling resources, hydrogen fuel derived from
         renewable resources, combined heat and power derived from renewable resources, and biomass resources.
